newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British dockers find unlikely allies in jobs fight.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British dockers find unlikely allies in jobs fight.

text.p: For most trade unionists, an old-style labour dispute in the Liverpool docks that has lasted a year with little economic impact and less media coverage epitomises the demise of union power in Britain.
For some left-wingers, however, it heralds the emergence of an alliance between those alienated by the modern Labour Party and single issue activists operating on the fringe of the political system.
In the latter camp is miners' leader Arthur Scargill, who formed the Socialist Labour Party earlier this year after Labour, the main opposition party, ditched its commitment to nationalisation.
"This is a turning point in politics," Scargill told a rally of some 2,000 people in the northern English port on September 28, a year to the day after the dock dispute began.

The man who a decade earlier had led almost 200,000 miners in a doomed, year-long strike to halt pit closures claimed to see a new beginning in the coming together of 329 dockers and a motley collection of animal rights activists, anti-roads protesters and rave party-goers.

Some of the dockers -- burly men dressed in denim, many of them over 50 -- seemed bemused by their new friends with coloured hair and nose studs, but Bobby Morton, one of their leaders, said he was not embarrassed.
"We invited them. They're all to do with the future. One of the reasons for the dispute is to protect the future of the kids in Liverpool, who we want to hand our jobs down to," he said.

The dispute began when men employed by Mersey Docks refused to cross a picket line set up by stevedores from a neighbouring port firm, who had been sacked in an overtime pay dispute. The dockers were then sacked.
On various occasions over the past year, Mersey Docks and Harbour Co has offered to reinstate some of the men -- up to 200 at one point -- with a pay-off and pensions for the rest.
The dockers have turned down each offer and none of the 329 has gone back to work -- a triumph of union solidarity according to them, the result of threats according to the company.
"The majority of the men are trapped outside by the picket line, and by the intimidation of the picket line," said Mersey Docks spokesman Eric Leatherbarrow.

Some 60 dockers and 900 other employees have worked throughout the dispute. All the dockers and 95 percent of the other employees are, like the 329, members of the Transport and General Workers Union (T&G).

The dispute cost the company four million pounds ($6.3 million) in 1995 and 600,000 pounds in the first half of 1996 but Leatherbarrow said costs are now minor, with new workers recruited and all terminals working normally since late 1995.
The dockers say the company provoked the dispute to replace long-serving employees with casual labour.
Leatherbarrow said the dockers engineered it with the aim of reviving the Dock Labour Scheme that effectively gave registered dockers a job for life until it was abolished in 1989.
"This is the final throw of the dinosaurs -- the small, militant nucleus that never wanted the scheme to go," he said.
The T&G has worked hard to broker a solution, and is alarmed by the arrival of the undisciplined elements in the eco-groups.
"We deplore the violence and unlawful action that has taken place," T&G leader Bill Morris said after some of them swarmed over port buildings and clashed with police.
The union has been hamstrung from the start by the fact that the dispute is illegal under the strict labour laws enacted by the Conservative government over the past 17 years.
Because the 329 never held a strike ballot, their refusal to cross the picket line constituted an illegal stoppage, and the T&G has had to refuse support or risk having funds sequestrated.
Scargill, repeating a demand turned down by the trade unions at their annual conference in September, called for a general strike every Wednesday until the dockers got their jobs back.

His main support at the conference came from the Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT). Several members of its ruling executive have joined Scargill's SLP and RMT assistant general secretary Bob Crow addressed the demonstrators in Liverpool.
"You can put up with the bosses' onslaught or get up off your knees and fight," he said.
The language at the rally was a far cry from the talk of "partnership with industry" espoused by new Labour under leader Tony Blair and the leadership of the Trades Union Congress umbrella body.
"We are going to oppose this capitalist system and pursue the goals of our mothers and fathers -- that is, socialism," said local dockers' leader Jimmy Nolan.
With Labour embracing market forces, primal anti-capitalism explains the unlikely coalition that has sprung up in Liverpool.

In a joint statement, the single issue groups said there was growing disillusion with mainstream politics "as the politicians gear up to present the electorate with a choice between two virtually indistinguishable political parties".
"Environmental sustainability and quality of life are higher values than the relentless pursuit of profits and economic growth," they said.
Or, as one banner put it, more succinctly: "New Labour = Slave Labour".
